text: From: ldantzker@comcast.net To: CClerk Cc: bstoff@fremont.gov; Christina Briggs; ralvardo@fremont.gov Subject: Charter Advisory Committee - Recruiting Top Executives in California Date: Thursday, April 16, 2026 12:07:02 PM Attachments: FremontDeptHeadAppts_2026-04-16_115938.pdf Council - City Manager Role in Recruiting Top Exec Talent.pdf Fremont City Clerk: Please forward the attached letter and document to the Fremont Charter Advisory Committee. Thank you, Lynn Dantzker Why Recruiting Top Executives in California Local Government Is So Difficult – The Impact of City Councils and City Managers California local governments face major challenges in attracting and retaining top talent at the executive level. Demographic, economic, and political forces have made recruiting city managers, department heads, and senior administrators harder than ever. ▪ The talent pipeline is shrinking. Baby Boomers who dominated local government leadership are retiring at an accelerating pace, and approximately 25–30% of the state and local government workforce is eligible for retirement within five years. Fewer mid-career professionals are choosing the path toward chief executive roles in public service. ▪ Competition from the private sector attracts talent. Top professionals in finance, technology, engineering, and human resources have more options than ever. The private sector offers competitive pay, workplace flexibility, and freedom from the political dynamics that define public-sector executive life. ▪ Public-sector executives work in a “fishbowl.” Every decision is subject to scrutiny and second-guessing on social media and at public meetings. Compensation is a source of criticism. Political volatility takes a personal toll. ▪ Cities have reputations. California local governments are closely connected. Experienced executives consult their networks before applying. Top-tier candidates will not apply in places where city councils are known for dysfunction, micromanagement, or disrespect of staff. City Council Plays a Critical Role A local government’s ability to attract and retain executive talent is either supported by or undermined by the behavior and culture of its governing body. Council dysfunction is the most frequently cited reason that top candidates decline to apply for or accept executive positions. Infighting, personal attacks, micromanagement, interference in administrative operations, and public mistreatment of staff send a signal to candidates that the environment is not conducive to professional management. High turnover in executive positions signals instability that experienced candidates recognize immediately. Councils that maintain a professional environment are places where executives want to work. This means: ▪ Treating professional staff as partners rather than political subordinates ▪ Enforce norms of civility and mutual respect ▪ Maintaining boundaries between governance and administration ▪ Investing in their own governance development ▪ Having strong, enforced non-interference policies or charter provisions ▪ Providing fair, competitive compensation ▪ Retaining stability during council transitions Every interaction between council members and staff is observed — at public meetings, in closed session, and on social media. The way a council treats its executives shapes the organization’s reputation across the entire profession. In a market where top candidates have choices, that reputation is the single most important factor in whether they apply. City Manager Sets the Tone The city manager is the person most responsible for building an internal culture and the leadership practices that make the organization a place where talented professionals choose to work — and choose to stay. This means that the city manager must: ▪ Constantly build an effective relationship with the Council. ▪ Foster trust, transparency, and mutual accountability throughout the organization. ▪ Operate as a cohesive unit with shared goals, open communication, and a commitment to supporting one another publicly and privately. ▪ Invest in professional development at every level. ▪ Advocate for competitive, equitable compensation ▪ Support modernization, strategic investment, and continuous improvement that reflects contemporary professional standards. Conclusion Recruiting top executive talent in California local government is a leadership, governance and human resources challenge. It is not just about putting up a job notice. In a shrinking talent market, reputation is currency. Every interaction, every public meeting, every decision about how staff are treated contributes to or detracts from the organization’s ability to compete for the people it needs. Sources Cal-ICMA, Preparing the Next Generation: A Guide for Current and Future Local Government Managers and Executives (ICMA, 2023). Center for State and Local Government Excellence, Workforce of the Future Survey (SLGE, 2024). Governing Magazine, “State and Local Governments Struggle to Attract Young Workers” (2024). International City/County Management Association (ICMA), Guidelines for Effective Governance (2023). League of California Cities, “Be an Employer of Choice: Local Government Workforce Strategies” (2024). section_title: 2. The Second Gate: Strategic Confirmation (City Council)
text: Date: Sunday, April 19, 2026 11:10:40 PM Bcc: City Manager and City Attorney Dear Charter Advisory Committee Members and City Staff, As we are discussing the Council's role in appointments, we must address two valid concerns: community’s vision. executives. We must avoid a system where department heads are hired based on political bias or personal loyalty rather than professional skill. To solve this, I propose that the Charter establish a Two-Gate Appointment System for "HighImpact" roles (Police Chief, Fire Chief, Public Works Director or similar high impact roles). The hiring process should remain led by the City Manager. The Manager has the executive skill to vet technical certifications, operational experience, and management history. The Goal: Ensure every finalist is 100% qualified to do the job. The Protection: This prevents a "political appointee" from being seated if they lack the necessary professional background. Once the City Manager has identified the top candidate, that individual must be confirmed by a majority vote of the City Council. * The Goal: The Council’s role is not to test their technical skills, but to ensure the candidate’s leadership philosophy and strategic priorities match the direction the voters have asked the Council to take. The Human Element: This allows the Council to ask the "Public Interest" questions: How will you address transparency? How do you view budget accountability? Consultative Interviews: Before a formal public vote, Council members should have the right to conduct individual or small-group interviews with the final candidate. This allows elected officials to gauge the candidate’s leadership style, responsiveness to community concerns, and alignment with the city's strategic goals. Formal Ratification: A final, public vote for confirmation. Why This is the Right Move for Fremont By using a Confirmation Model rather than a Direct Appointment Model, we protect the city in three ways: Avoids Micro-management: The Council doesn't spend time reviewing resumes or conducting first-round interviews. They stay in their lane as "Elected Representatives." Prevents Silos: It ensures the City Manager can still manage their team effectively, as the Council can only approve or reject the Manager’s choice they cannot force their own choice on the Manager. Increases Public Trust: For high-stakes roles like the Police Chief or Public Works Director, a public confirmation vote provides a layer of transparency that a closed-door hiring by a single manager cannot match. Bridging the Skill Gap: This allows the Council to act as Elected Representatives rather than "Technical Managers." They don't need to be engineers to judge if a Public Works Director is transparent and communicative. Building the Relationship: A department head who has met 1-on-1 with their Council is far more likely to be a collaborative partner than one who is hired in a "silo" by the City Manager. Avoiding Political Bias: Because the City Manager still controls the selection of the candidate, the Council cannot just pick a personal favorite. The interview serves as a "Check and Balance" to ensure the Manager’s choice is truly a fit for the whole city. I urge the committee to consider a "Manager-Initiated, Council-Confirmed" model in the draft Charter. It provides a bridge between professional expertise and democratic accountability. Thanks vipin From: NMAP Archives To: councilmeetings Subject: Public Comment Charter Advisory Committee 4/20/26 Date: Monday, April 20, 2026 12:57:38 PM After multiple meetings, the Committee continues to circle around basic governance questions while advancing conclusions that have not been earned. Two points now stand out clearly:

section_title: 2. The Committee has not identified a system failure that necessitates immediate structural change.
text: failure. Recent discussion has centered on increasing council pay, transitioning to full-time roles, and adding dedicated staff. These are not minor adjustments. They redefine the role of elected office. Yet after weeks of meetings, there is still no clear statement of what the current system cannot accomplish. The argument that councilmembers should be compensated as fulltime officials because they currently hold full-time jobs elsewhere does not hold. That is a personal choice, not a structural defect. The position was accepted with a defined compensation structure and role expectation. Choosing to allocate more time to the role does not convert it into a different office. If the position is now being redefined, that needs to be justified on public need, not personal workload preferences. If workload is the issue, the committee must define it. If responsiveness is the issue, then the committe should measure it. How many constituent requests go unanswered? What response time is expected? What accountability exists today, and what specifically is missing? None of these questions have been answered. Without that, a proposal to increase compensation reads as self-serving. It benefits the very body that would ultimately approve it, without establishing a public return. Disagreements over policy outcomes are not evidence of a broken governance model. They reflect differences in judgment. A charter is not catch-all magic wand to resolve those differences by personalizing an outcome through policy fiat. Even staff has acknowledged that some of the items being discussed can be addressed within the current framework. That raises a simple question: what specifically cannot be done today? That question remains unanswered. Simultaneously, the Committee is being asked to consider changes that carry ongoing fiscal impact. Increased compensation and additional staffing are recurring obligations. Where is the analysis tying those costs to measurable improvements? What outcome improves, and by how much?Without a defined problem, cost projections and compensation comparisons do not establish necessity. They only establish preference. Until the Committee can clearly state what has failed, what cannot be accomplished under the current structure, and why those limitations exist, advancing compensation and staffing proposals is premature and lacks a defensible basis. Right now, the sequence is backwards. Conclusions are being explored before the problem has been defined. At best, it is outcome-seeking. At worst, it is council-approved exploration of self-enrichment. Both interpretations produce poor optics on the charter process and done so at the taxpayers' expense. Surely, this cannot be the defining moment the Committee looked forward to where high-level criticisms of current structure is reduced to a recommendation of a minor salary bump. If that is the only conclusion the Committee has distilled, then the answer is before you on whether a charter should exist.
